sources.publisher: UCSF Department of Otolaryngology — Head and Neck Surgery
sources.title: Surgery (Before, During, and After) & Post-Operative Care
passage_locations: What is the healing process and post-operative care like?
When should I call my doctor following surgery?

claims.claim: The patient or a family member removes the mastoid dressing two days after surgery.
When tape is not present, clean the incision edges gently twice each day with equal parts hydrogen peroxide and distilled water, then apply an over-the-counter antibiotic ointment such as bacitracin.
When tape covers the incision, keep the area dry for three days and do not clean the wound during that period.
The patient may shower and wash their hair three days after surgery.
A post-operative wound check and ear exam occurs approximately two weeks after surgery.
The sutures dissolve and do not need removal.
Notify the surgeon or clinic when the wound is red and swollen, does not improve over the next one to two days, and is painful to touch.
Notify the surgeon or clinic for a fever greater than 101.5 degrees Fahrenheit.
Notify the surgeon or clinic for swelling behind the ear or a feeling that fluid is collecting under the skin behind the ear.
Notify the surgeon or clinic for headache, light sensitivity, or excessive lethargy after surgery.
Contact the surgeon or clinic for wound-care questions or medical concerns about the patient or child.

sources.publisher: UCSF Department of Otolaryngology — Head and Neck Surgery
sources.title: Emergency Contact

claims.claim: For routine clinic or surgeon questions, leave a message on the nursing line at 415-353-2148.
The public page says to expect a call back within 12 hours and to call again if no call is received.
For an emergency, call the hospital operator at 415-476-1000 and ask for the Otolaryngology resident on call.

sources.publisher: UCSF Department of Otolaryngology — Head and Neck Surgery
sources.title: Cochlear Implantation Activation
passage_locations: What happens after the cochlear implantation surgery?

claims.claim: After a healing period, the patient returns for programming of the externally worn speech processor.
Each speech-processor program is customized for the user.
Later visits include implant and equipment checks, performance measurement, and continued follow-up.

sources.publisher: UCSF Department of Otolaryngology — Head and Neck Surgery
sources.title: Timeline of Appointments

claims.claim: This document places surgeon healing review and audiology activation two to three weeks after surgery, which conflicts with the activation page's about-one-month wording.
The post-operative timeline says the patient meets with an audiologist for device activation.
Several later post-operative audiology visits are used to fine-tune the device.

modules.title: Care for the surgery site

canonical_sentences.text: Two days after surgery, remove the mastoid dressing, or head bandage.
Next, check whether tape covers the incision, or surgical cut, behind the ear.
If there is tape, keep the area dry until three days after surgery.
Do not clean the incision before that time.
If there is no tape, clean the edges of the incision gently twice a day.
Use a mix of equal parts hydrogen peroxide and distilled water.
Then apply an over-the-counter antibiotic ointment, such as bacitracin.
Three days after surgery, you may shower and wash your hair.
Your wound check and ear exam are about two weeks after surgery.
The stitches dissolve, so they do not need to be removed.

modules.visual_policy: Text-only until the partner surgeon approves any wound-care illustration or animation.

modules.title: When to call

canonical_sentences.text: Call your surgeon or clinic staff if all three signs below are present.
The incision is red and swollen.
It does not get better over the next one to two days.
It hurts when touched.
Call if you have a fever above 101.5 degrees Fahrenheit.
Call if the skin behind your ear is swollen or feels like fluid is building up under it.
Call if you have a headache, light sensitivity, or excessive lethargy.
Call if you have a wound-care question or another medical concern about you or your child.
For routine questions for the clinic or surgeon, leave a message on the nursing line at 415-353-2148.
The UCSF page says you should get a call within 12 hours.
If no one calls, call again.
For an emergency, call 415-476-1000 and ask for the Otolaryngology resident on call.

structured_values.logic: red AND swollen AND not improving AND painful to touch

modules.visual_policy: Warnings remain complete text. No visual may grade severity or assign an urgency tier without surgeon approval.

modules.phase: after the surgery site has healed
modules.title: Your first programming visits

canonical_sentences.text: After the surgery site has healed, you return for your first programming visit.
At the visit, a hearing specialist called an audiologist programs the speech processor you wear outside your ear.
The program is made for your needs.
At later visits, the team checks the implant and equipment and measures how they are working.
You will keep returning for checks and fine-tuning.

structured_values.conflict: public activation page says about one month; public timeline says two to three weeks

modules.visual_policy: Show only nonclinical orientation until the partner surgeon approves processor, implant-location, or activation illustrations.
